Charon. Pluto's largest moon and so massive relative to its primary that the two bodies orbit around a shared center of gravity called a barycenter, making them functionally a binary system. Discovered in nineteen seventy-eight, Charon is half the diameter of Pluto, and together they were reclassified as dwarf planets in two thousand six.

Charon is about twelve hundred twelve kilometers in diameter, which makes it about half the size of Pluto and the largest moon relative to its primary of any body in the solar system. The two worlds face each other tidally locked, and they orbit their common barycenter every six point three nine days at an inclination of ninety-nine point seven degrees, which tilts Pluto's rotation axis dramatically. James W. Christy discovered Charon in nineteen seventy-eight using photographic plates from the United States Naval Observatory.

Geologically, Charon turns out to be far more complex than its size might suggest. The surface shows cratered highlands, smooth plains, and evidence of past volcanism and tectonics. A dark equatorial zone and bright polar caps of water ice suggest compositional variations across the moon.

The New Horizons spacecraft flyby in two thousand fifteen provided the first high-resolution images of Charon, revealing its intricate surface geology and confirming its role as one of the clearest examples of a moon-planet binary in the solar system. Both Pluto and Charon are denizens of the outer solar system in the Kuiper Belt.
